episode_title: Six More Stories That Should Be Films

stories.title: Swimming for IIT
stories.description: Ajay's fictional story where IIT entrance is based on swimming. A boy who loves engineering is forced to learn swimming, gets disillusioned, finds joy in open sea swimming, fails the exam, and disappears into the sea.

stories.title: The Lost Plutonium of Nanda Devi
stories.description: Amit's true story about a CIA-Indian Intelligence mission to place a plutonium-powered listening device on Nanda Devi to spy on China. The device was lost in a storm and might still be sinking through the glacier, posing a threat to the Ganges.

stories.title: Delhi College (1803-1857)
stories.description: Ajay's non-fiction story about the cultural ferment in Delhi before 1857. It features the clash of Persian and English/Urdu, the rationalist mathematician Ramchandra, and the vibrant poetry scene.

stories.title: The Scuttling at Scapa Flow
stories.description: Amit's true story about the German High Seas Fleet scuttling itself in 1919 to avoid surrender. The steel from these ships was later salvaged for Geiger counters because it was free of post-1945 background radiation.

stories.title: The Vlogger's Mexican Standoff
stories.description: Ajay's fictional 'found footage' story about vloggers. It involves a 'Mexican standoff' of cameras and a vlogger falling in love with an androgynous character who might be the only 'real' person in a fake world.

stories.title: Parachuting Sheep
stories.description: Amit's scene from the Italian invasion of Ethiopia (1935) where live sheep were parachuted to feed mutinous soldiers who demanded good Italian food.

recommendations.comment: Swapna Liddle's book about Delhi from 1803 to 1857, which inspired Ajay's story.
A poem by Stevie Smith, recited by Ajay to end his swimming story.

core_ideas.description: Ajay's swimming story illustrates how any metric used for selection (like swimming for IIT) will eventually be gamed, defeating its original purpose.
The lost plutonium on Nanda Devi and the low-background steel from Scapa Flow show how actions can have long-lasting, unforeseen effects on the world.
The shift from Persian to English/Urdu in 19th-century Delhi shows how language dictates power and how rapid shifts can leave entire generations stranded.
The discussion on vloggers and 'character is contingent' suggests that true authenticity might be impossible, as we are always adapting to our context.
